# mediamix

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/elkronos/mediamix/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/elkronos/mediamix/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
<!-- badges: end -->

Composable media transforms and attribution path construction for R.

**Documentation, walkthroughs and worked examples:
<https://elkronos.github.io/mediamix/>**

mediamix turns raw marketing data into model-ready features: media spend into
carryover- and saturation-adjusted regressors, and raw event logs into
attributed customer journeys.

It is a preprocessing, feature-engineering and reporting package, not a
modelling engine. `lm()`, `glmnet` and `brms` fit models better than a
marketing package would, and `tune` does hyperparameter search properly.
mediamix does the steps in front of the model and the decomposition after it,
with the methodological details that usually get skipped written into the API.

## Installation

mediamix is not yet on CRAN. Install the development version from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("elkronos/mediamix")
```

`pak` does not build vignettes for packages installed from GitHub, so
`vignette("carryover")` and the others are not available after this install.
Read them on the [package website](https://elkronos.github.io/mediamix/), or
install with `remotes::install_github("elkronos/mediamix", build_vignettes = TRUE)`.

## What it offers

The full MMM frameworks (Robyn in R; Meridian and PyMC-Marketing in Python)
bundle transforms, a model, an optimiser and reporting into one pipeline.
mediamix provides those pieces separately, for use around a model you choose:
your own `lm()`, `brms` or `glmnet` model, a `tidymodels` workflow, or a Stan
model.

- **Adstock that survives resampling.** `step_adstock()` carries filter state
  across the train/test boundary, so carryover, saturation and a model penalty
  can be tuned jointly in one `tune_bayes()` call with no rows lost.
- **Marginal ROI done by counterfactual.** `marginal_roi()` re-runs the whole
  transform on a 1% larger budget, the definition used in Google's MMM
  research and Meridian. The common shortcut, a curve's slope times the
  kernel's first weight, understates slow channels several-fold.
- **Carryover selection with honest uncertainty.** `tune_carryover()` and,
  for every channel at once inside one model with controls,
  `tune_carryover_joint()` score candidates on held-out KPI with forward-only
  resampling and report the one-standard-error choice alongside the minimum.
- **Intervals, not just point estimates.** `block_bootstrap()` resamples runs
  of weeks to put intervals on ROI, marginal ROI or anything else you compute.
- **Journeys as a first-class step.** `build_paths()` turns a raw event log
  into journeys with every construction choice an argument, and accounts for
  the conversions that filtering leaves unattributable.
- **Heuristic and data-driven attribution side by side.** Five rule-based
  credit schemes and an order-1 Markov removal-effect model, with
  `attribution_spread()` reporting how much the answer depends on the choice.

## A light dependency footprint

mediamix imports `cli` and `rlang` for its messages and `data.table` for the
attribution half, where event logs get large. It has no compiled code.
`recipes`, `dials` and the rest of tidymodels are in `Suggests` and registered
conditionally, so the transforms work equally well from a Stan or `brms`
workflow that will never touch them.

```{r}
library(mediamix)

adstock_geometric(c(100, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0), decay = 0.5)
```

## The half-life vocabulary

Practitioners say "television works for about three weeks". They do not say
"television has a decay coefficient of 0.7937". The package translates, and
uses one vocabulary throughout:

```{r}
theta <- decay_from_half_life(3)
theta
half_life(theta)
effective_window(theta, 0.90)
```

That last line is how you decide whether your data can identify a carryover
this long: a decay implying a 40-week effective window on 104 weeks of data
cannot be estimated, however confident the cross-validation looks.

## Journey construction as a first-class step

Attribution tools such as `ChannelAttribution` consume `"a > b > c"` strings
with conversion counts attached; producing those strings is left to the
analyst. That step usually ends up as a `group_by()` and a
`paste(collapse = " > ")`, and that loses a great deal.

```{r journey-table, echo = FALSE}
data(mm_events)
ordered <- mm_events[order(mm_events$customer_id, mm_events$timestamp), ]
naive <- split(ordered$channel, ordered$customer_id)
step <- function(...) {
  s <- path_summary(suppressMessages(build_paths(
    mm_events, id = "customer_id", channel = "channel",
    timestamp = "timestamp", conversion = "conversion", ...)))
  c(s$journeys, s$mean_length)
}
steps <- rbind(
  "naive one-path-per-customer" = c(length(naive), mean(lengths(naive))),
  "split on conversion" = step(split_on = "conversion",
                               collapse_repeats = FALSE),
  "+ 30-day inactivity gap" = step(split_on = c("conversion", "gap"), gap = 30,
                                   collapse_repeats = FALSE),
  "+ collapse consecutive duplicates" = step(split_on = c("conversion", "gap"),
                                             gap = 30, collapse_repeats = TRUE)
)
more <- round(100 * (steps[4, 1] / steps[1, 1] - 1))
shorter <- round(100 * (1 - steps[4, 2] / steps[1, 2]))
```

On the package's `r format(nrow(mm_events), big.mark = ",")`-event synthetic
log:

```{r journey-table-print, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  ` ` = rownames(steps),
  journeys = format(steps[, 1], big.mark = ","),
  `mean length` = sprintf("%.2f", steps[, 2]),
  check.names = FALSE
), align = c("l", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE)
```

`r more`% more journeys, `r shorter`% shorter. Journey counts and lengths feed
a Markov transition matrix directly, so those are not rounding differences.

```{r}
paths <- build_paths(
  mm_events,
  id = "customer_id", channel = "channel", timestamp = "timestamp",
  conversion = "conversion", value = "value",
  lookback = 30,                       # or read it off conversion_lag()
  split_on = c("conversion", "gap"), gap = 30,
  collapse_repeats = TRUE,
  keep_null_paths = TRUE,              # Markov removal effects need these
  direct = "label"
)
```

`build_paths()` handles the things that go wrong between an event log and a
set of journeys: journey splitting, lookback windows, non-converting paths,
direct, none and missing channels, consecutive duplicates, duplicate events,
timestamps that do not parse, deterministic tie-breaking, and accounting for
conversions that filtering leaves unattributable. Each is an argument, not an
assumption.

Dropping direct traffic can strip a converting journey of every touchpoint it
had. mediamix fixes the conversion facts before any filtering, so those
conversions are counted and reported as `conversions_unattributable` rather
than quietly shrinking the denominator.

## The spread is the finding

Any single credit rule gives you a number. Several give you the range that
number could have been. `attribute()` runs five heuristic rules and an order-1
Markov removal-effect model (Anderl et al., 2016). The four channels whose
share varies most:

```{r}
shares <- attribute(paths)
spread <- attribution_spread(shares)
head(spread, 4)
```

```{r attribution}
plot(shares)
```

```{r spread-facts, include = FALSE}
display <- spread[spread$channel == "display", ]
heuristic <- shares[shares$rule != "markov", ]
markov <- shares[shares$rule == "markov", ]
inside <- vapply(markov$channel, function(ch) {
  h <- heuristic$share[heuristic$channel == ch]
  m <- markov$share[markov$channel == ch]
  m >= min(h) && m <= max(h)
}, logical(1))
```

Display's share runs from `r round(100 * display$min_share)`% to
`r round(100 * display$max_share)`% depending only on the convention chosen.
That channel has not been measured; it has been assigned a number. The Markov
share falls inside the heuristic range for `r sum(inside)` of
`r length(inside)` channels here: a data-driven convention narrows the
argument without ending it.

## The conceptual spine

Adstock takes one impulse of spend and spreads its effect *forward* with
geometric decay. Time-decay attribution takes one conversion and spreads its
credit *backward* with the same kernel. The arithmetic is the same and the
arrow is reversed, and in the API both use the same `decay` argument, per
period of the series for adstock and per `period` of elapsed time for credit:

```{r}
# One evenly spaced four-touch journey
j <- data.frame(
  cust = "a", channel = c("display", "social", "email", "paid_search"),
  ts = as.POSIXct("2026-01-01", tz = "UTC") + (0:3) * 86400,
  conv = c(0, 0, 0, 1)
)
one <- build_paths(j, id = "cust", channel = "channel",
                   timestamp = "ts", conversion = "conv")

adstock_weights(max_lag = 4, decay = 0.5)

rev(credit_time_decay(one, decay = 0.5)$credit)

all.equal(adstock_weights(4, 0.5), rev(credit_time_decay(one, decay = 0.5)$credit))
```

For the geometric kernel on evenly spaced touches the two are identical. See
`vignette("spine")`, which also sets out where the symmetry stops.

## Carryover parameters chosen against the KPI

It is tempting to choose decay by asking which transformed series is
best-behaved. That criterion has no dependent variable in it, so it ranks
filters by how hard they smooth rather than by anything about the outcome.

`tune_carryover()` scores each candidate by how well a model predicts
*held-out KPI*. The default model is ordinary least squares; `fit_fn` and
`predict_fn` take any other.

```{r}
data(mm_weekly)
north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
controls <- data.frame(week = seq_len(nrow(north)), price = north$price,
                       seasonality = north$seasonality,
                       holiday = north$holiday)

tuned <- tune_carryover(north$tv, north$revenue, controls = controls,
                        decays = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05))
tuned$best       # the minimum of the cross-validation curve
tuned$best_1se   # the shortest carryover within one standard error of it
```

With several channels, tune them together so none is credited with another's
effect, and pass the controls, which stay aligned with every split:

```{r}
joint <- tune_carryover_joint(north[channels], north$revenue,
                              controls = controls)
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")$decay[channels]
rbind(estimate = joint$best$decay, truth = truth)
```

```{r joint-facts, include = FALSE}
off <- channels[round(abs(joint$best$decay - truth), 8) > 0.1]
```

Of the five, `r knitr::combine_words(off)` miss by more than 0.1. Search's
cross-validation profile is almost flat: the data does not identify its
carryover, which `plot(joint)` makes visible and a bare point estimate would
hide.

The test suite simulates data from a known decay and requires it to be
recovered to within one grid step at every value tested. Carryover is weakly
identified in most real data, which is why the one-standard-error rule
(Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, 2009) is reported alongside. See
`vignette("carryover")`, which also shows how much harder this gets with five
correlated channels and 156 weeks, and why that is a fact about the model
rather than about the objective.

## Recipe steps that survive the train/test boundary

A lag built with `recipes::step_lag()` leaves `NA`, or the filler given as its
`default`, in the first rows of new data at every prep/bake boundary, and
dropping those rows removes the boundary weeks from training and evaluation.

`step_adstock()` carries the filter across the boundary instead. `prep()`
stores each group's training time points and media values, and `bake()`
continues the filter from them, so new data that follows or repeats the end of
the training series gets exactly the values of a whole-series filter. Row
count and order are preserved.

```r
recipe(revenue ~ ., data = train) |>
  step_adstock(all_of(channels), index = "date", by = "geo", decay = tune()) |>
  step_saturation(all_of(channels), half_max = tune(), shape = tune())
```

`bake()` classifies the new data against what `prep()` saw (contiguous,
overlapping, after a gap, out of step with the training periods, or an unseen
group) and continues the filter only when that is correct, warning otherwise.
This is what makes joint tuning of carryover, saturation and model penalty
possible in one `tune_bayes()` call. Each step takes one `decay`, so add one
step per channel, with `all_of(!!ch)` in a loop, to give every channel its own
tunable carryover.

## Marginal return on spend

Average ROI is a scorecard; marginal ROI is the decision variable.
`marginal_roi()` computes it the way the Bayesian MMM literature defines it,
as the extra response from a 1% larger budget divided by the extra spend, by
re-running carryover and saturation rather than differentiating a curve:

```{r}
tv <- marginal_roi(north$tv, coefficient = 6013,
                   adstock = list(decay = 0.85),
                   saturation = list(half_max = 2250, shape = 1.6))
tv
```

```{r shortcut, include = FALSE}
z <- adstock_geometric(north$tv, decay = 0.85)
shortcut <- mroi(mean(z), coefficient = 6013, half_max = 2250, shape = 1.6) *
  (1 - 0.85)
```

The tempting shortcut, the curve's slope times the kernel's first weight,
gives `r round(shortcut, 2)` for this channel: it counts only the week of
spend and discards the 85% of the effect that arrives later.

The main results have `plot()` methods in one consistent,
colour-vision-checked style. Here is the decomposition that `contributions()`
returns:

```{r contributions, echo = FALSE}
spec_media <- as.data.frame(Map(function(x, d, h, s) media_transform(
  x, adstock = list(decay = d), saturation = list(half_max = h, shape = s)),
  north[channels], attr(mm_weekly, "truth")$decay[channels],
  attr(mm_weekly, "truth")$half_max[channels],
  attr(mm_weekly, "truth")$shape[channels]))
fit <- lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = cbind(spec_media, controls))
plot(contributions(spec_media, fit, index = north$date))
```

And `block_bootstrap()` puts intervals on any of it. On `mm_weekly` they are
wide, which is the point: see the
[budget walkthrough](https://elkronos.github.io/mediamix/articles/budget-walkthrough.html)
for how that changes a recommendation, and how its answer compares with the
truth the data was simulated from.

## Scope

| In | Out | Because |
|---|---|---|
| Adstock and saturation transforms | Model fitting | `lm`, `glmnet`, `brms` already exist |
| Carryover selection by cross-validation | Bespoke optimisers | `tune` does this properly |
| Journey construction from event logs | Higher-order Markov chains | `ChannelAttribution` does them in C++ |
| Rule-based credit and order-1 Markov removal effects | Causal incrementality | Requires experiments, not logs |
| Contribution, ROI and counterfactual marginal ROI | Budget optimisation | Deserves its own design pass |
| Media data diagnostics | Generic regression diagnostics | `broom`, `performance` |

`as_channel_paths()` exports journeys straight into `ChannelAttribution`'s
format, for higher-order models and very large path tables.

## Attribution is a convention

Rule-based attribution is a bookkeeping convention, not a causal estimate. It
divides observed conversions among observed touchpoints by a rule you chose; it
cannot tell you what would have happened if a channel had not run, because that
outcome is not in the log. Only an experiment answers that.
